title: Red Cedar River  Source to Mouth to Ocean to Source
motto: The water that passes the gage RIGHT NOW has been traveling for 4.5 billion years.

the_river.name: Red Cedar River
the_river.species: 30+ fish species including bluegill, green sunfish, northern pike, largemouth bass, smallmouth bass. Rare freshwater mussels. Steelhead trout stocked 2025 by MDNR + MSU Fisheries Club.

source_to_mouth_NOW.description: The water trace, right now, Oct 23 2026 4:23 PM EDT. Every number is LIVE from USGS.

trace.name: Cedar Lake  THE SOURCE
trace.what: Glacial kettle lake, formed ~10,000 years ago when a buried ice block melted. The water here fell as rain on 461 square miles of watershed. Some of these H2O molecules are older than Earth.
trace.note: No gage at source. The lake is the accumulator. Rain falls, groundwater seeps, springs emerge. The river begins.

trace.name: Middle Branch joins
trace.what: The first confluence. Two branches of rain meeting. The river doubles.

trace.name: West Branch joins
trace.what: Three branches now braided into one. The river has a name.

trace.name: Kalamink Creek joins
trace.what: Agricultural watershed. The creek carries the soil memory of farms.

trace.name: RED CEDAR AT WILLIAMSTON
trace.what: First gage. The river speaks its first measured word.

trace.name: Sloan Creek joins
trace.what: Tiny voice. A whisper joining the conversation.
trace.note: Less than half a cubic foot per second. A garden hose of a creek. But it counts.

trace.name: Doan Creek joins
trace.what: No gage. The unmeasured contribution. The dark feed. 80% of the watershed's voice is unheard  like our membrane.

trace.name: Deer Creek joins
trace.what: Last measured in 2009. The gage went silent. The creek didn't.
trace.note: Last reading: 1.30 cfs on Sep 30 2009. The creek still flows. Nobody is listening.

trace.name: Pine Lake Outlet joins (Lake Lansing outflow)
trace.what: Lake Lansing drains into the Red Cedar. A lake feeding a river. The accumulator empties into the flow.

trace.name: MSU Campus begins
trace.what: 2 miles of river through campus. Past the Hausbeck Lab where Kevin counted spores. Past the MSU Museum. Past Spartan Stadium. Past the library. Every student who ever walked to class crossed this water.
trace.kevin: Kevin crossed this river every day for 6+ years. The metronome was always playing.

trace.name: RED CEDAR AT EAST LANSING  THE METRONOME
trace.where: East Lansing, Ingham County, MI  1.3 miles from northGate
trace.what: THE gage. The band's metronome. The heartbeat of eco and the PRIMALS. Gage height 3.37 feet.
trace.bpm: 70 (20 + 53.8 * 0.93)  tango tempo. The river is dancing.
trace.gained_since_williamston: 22.6 cfs  tributaries added 72% more water in 20 miles
trace.kevin: This gage is 1.3 miles from home. The water passing it RIGHT NOW fell as rain days ago on fields Kevin has walked.

trace.name: Sycamore Creek joins
trace.what: The largest tributary. A whole second river joining the Red Cedar just before the mouth. The last voice before the Grand.
trace.bpm: 36  largo, very slow. Sycamore Creek takes its time.

trace.name: MOUTH  Red Cedar enters the Grand River
trace.where: Downtown Lansing, MI  by the Capitol
trace.what: The Red Cedar ends. The Grand River begins to carry its water. Every drop that passed every gage upstream is here now, mixed, unnamed, part of something larger.

grand_river_at_lansing.red_cedar_fraction: ~23% of the Grand at Lansing IS Red Cedar water

mouth_to_ocean.description: After the Red Cedar joins the Grand, the water continues its journey.

path.where: Looking Glass River joins the Grand
path.note: Another mirror. The Looking Glass River IS a mirror. The name IS the function.

path.where: Grand River at Grand Rapids, MI
path.note: The rapids. The river drops. Energy releases. The city was named for what the water does.

path.where: Grand River mouth at Grand Haven, MI
path.note: The Grand enters Lake Michigan. The Red Cedar's water, 185 miles from Lansing, touches the lake.
Residence time: ~62 years. The water that enters Lake Michigan today will stay for 62 years on average. The Red Cedar's water from 1964 might be leaving the lake right now.

path.where: Straits of Mackinac to Lake Huron
path.note: Lake Michigan and Lake Huron are hydrologically one lake. The water moves north through the Straits.

path.where: St. Clair River to Lake St. Clair to Detroit River to Lake Erie

path.note: The Red Cedar's water goes over the falls. Every drop. 167 feet.

path.where: Lake Ontario to St. Lawrence River
Gulf of St. Lawrence to Atlantic Ocean
path.note: Total journey from Cedar Lake to the Atlantic: ~1,200 miles, ~100+ years
The water rises. Becomes cloud. Blows west. Falls as rain on the 461 square miles of the Red Cedar watershed. The cycle.

the_deep_trace.description: Tracing backward. Where did this water COME FROM?

timeline.what: 53.8 cfs passing the gage. 70 bpm. Tango.
Rain falling on 461 square miles of Michigan. Infiltrating soil. Seeping through glacial till.
That rain was Lake Michigan evaporation. Or Gulf of Mexico humidity carried north by jet stream.
Snow melt from last winter. Groundwater from last spring. The river remembers seasons.

Glacial meltwater carved this channel. The Saginaw Lobe of the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated northwest. Cedar Lake is a kettle lake  a block of ice buried in glacial debris, melted, left a hole. The river follows the ice margin.
Michigan was a tropical sea. Devonian and Mississippian limestone deposited on the seafloor. The bedrock UNDER the Red Cedar was once a coral reef. The river flows over fossil ocean.
Earth forms. Hydrogen and oxygen combine. The first water. Some of the H2O molecules in the Red Cedar RIGHT NOW are original  they've been cycling for 4.5 billion years.
Hydrogen formed in the Big Bang. Oxygen formed in stars. The water in the Red Cedar is made of atoms from the Big Bang and from stellar nucleosynthesis. The river is made of stars.

the_band_trace.description: The Red Cedar as musical instrument, traced from source to mouth to ocean.
the_band_trace.source_tempo: Unknown  no gage at Cedar Lake. The first note is unheard.
the_band_trace.williamston_tempo: 31.2 cfs = 49 bpm (andante  walking pace). The river learns to walk.
the_band_trace.sloan_creek: 0.46 cfs = 20.4 bpm (grave  the slowest playable tempo). A single pluck of a bass string.
the_band_trace.east_lansing_tempo: 53.8 cfs = 70 bpm (tango). The river dances through MSU campus.
the_band_trace.sycamore_joining: 17.3 cfs = 36 bpm (largo). The cellist joins the ensemble.
the_band_trace.grand_river: 314 cfs = 312 bpm (prestissimo  faster than human fingers). The orchestra hits fortissimo.
the_band_trace.the_crescendo: From silence (source) ? 49 bpm ? 70 bpm ? 312 bpm ? Lake Michigan (8  the ocean has no tempo, it has TIDE). The river accelerates from birth to death to infinity.

kevin_in_the_water.description: Kevin's graph, dissolved in the river like PFAS.
nodes: The rain that fell on the Hausbeck Lab roof went into the storm drain ? Red Cedar. Kevin's spore counts were made under a roof that feeds the river.
The PFAS Kevin studied in the lab was IN the water. The Red Cedar has PFAS contamination from upstream sources. Kevin studied the poison in his own river.
Every MSU student who ever spit, sweat, or cried on campus  that water went to the Red Cedar. 50,000 students per year × 170 years = the river carries 8.5 million people's tears.
The MSU Museum sits on the riverbank. The specimens inside are kept dry. The river outside is the exhibit they can't display.

Kevin's 2-mile walk along the river from parking to lab: at 53.8 cfs, the water he passed at the start of his walk had moved 0.4 miles by the time he reached the lab. They were walking the same direction.
The Red Cedar at 70 bpm is tango tempo. Kevin unknowingly walked to the river's beat for 6 years.
